8.en: The following sections discuss the Inquisition’s place in the Imperium: the truth of an Inquisitor’s limitless authority, what laws they must adhere to, and how they deal with the multitudinous factions of the Adeptus Terra and beyond. Some of these aspects have been outlined in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.tFbQS9Pwk46yjwFq]{The Holy Orders of the Inquisition Player’s Guide} to instil knowledge required by players and their acolyte characters. Rather, the following information is for the benefit of GMs to understand better the Inquisitors they roleplay and the limits of these powerful and enigmatic characters.

16.en: While their means and methods vary wildly, all Inquisitors have a limitless authority. In theory, this is absolute; they can commandeer any resources they might need and command everyone from the heads of noble houses to decorated generals of the Astra Militarum to work on their behalf.

20.en: In practice, however, Inquisitors must constantly fight for their authority to count as such. The galaxy is vast and far from Terra, and an Inquisitor may find themself at the edge of the God-Emperor’s influence. Even on worlds that pay their tithes to the God-Emperor, the governors may claim the Inquisition is no better than a myth or recognise their authority without significant backup. Often, Inquisitors can rely only on themselves.

24.en: The work of an Inquisitor sometimes requires making enemies as well as friends, and the nature of their foes often means that the longer an Inquisitor pursues their prey, the more they are tempted, tested, and possibly even tainted. So the more power and resources an Inquisitor accumulates, the more Liabilities they have. Working out an Inquisitorial Patron’s history leads to adding certain Boons and Liabilities, or, if preferred, selecting Boons and Liabilities might naturally inspire a particular backstory.

34.en: For characters who play Inquisitorial agents, the route from lowly acolyte to Inquisitor or beyond is a long and dangerous road that might take several lifetimes to achieve. To preserve knowledge and skills in an organisation as secretive and dispersed as the Inquisition, rejuvenat extends the life of the most esteemed members. Anyone who has lasted long enough to reach a position of supreme power and influence in the Inquisition is unlikely to be superseded soon. Some Inquisitors train acolytes to join their fight as fully-fledged Interrogators, but few take more than one or two at a time, and success is never guaranteed. For these characters, having an Inquisitor as a Patron might be the next best thing to a personal mentor, and impressing their Patron might even improve their standing with the Inquisition.

44.en: Members of Ordos Majoris might have access to the data and resources of their Ordo when preparing for a mission, but less so once a mission is underway. Inquisitors are powerful, but they are still individual mortals standing against a hostile galaxy of nightmarish foes. Theoretically, any Inquisitor can ask for help from another in those rare cases when they meet, but even Inquisitors of the same Ordo cannot afford to trust unquestioningly.

48.en: It is often safer for an Inquisitor to commandeer staff as necessary in their work, individuals whose ignorance makes them easier to control. Some of these are used and discarded, while those proven loyal and useful become acolytes. Acolytes face the same horrors as their superiors but operate without the benefit of experience and only second-hand authority from their Inquisitor while in the field.

52.en: In the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96]{Macharian Sector}, the most successful Inquisitors tend to learn all they can about the sector and its significant players and then set themselves on gaining personal power and influence within. Inquisitors who have been in the sector longest have had time to develop networks, make contacts, and earn favours. Some work alone with nothing but their personal weapon to rely on or recruit a small, select team, while others may have Inquisitorial training facilities or a null-prison available, a large staff and military force, sanctioned psykers, vast databanks, voidships, and a seemingly endless fortune of solars.

56.en: If the characters’ Patron is an Inquisitor, then their Boons make clear the resources they can make available. Since an Inquisitor who works alone and undercover is less likely to become a Patron than one with means and influence, they likely have something to offer the characters, and the more solars they have at their disposal, the more likely they are to pay the characters well.

70.en: Many acts of Inquisitors and their agents are never revealed to the masses, but the Inquisition is said to have eyes everywhere. Whenever a character prevents a catastrophe, destroys a shipment of xenos weapons, or exposes a cult, there is a surprisingly good chance that the Inquisition will eventually become aware of it.

74.en: Many Patrons monitor their agents closely, but even if a particular Patron does not communicate with an Ordo, there are other ways the Inquisition might find out. Either another Inquisitor will have been conducting a similar investigation and share the report with their Ordo, or an Inquisitor’s contacts in the Arbites or local police force might inform them after the fact.

78.en: Messages and reports take significant time to cross the Imperium, but most Inquisitors keep meticulous records and are always interested in promising agents or contacts. Many Inquisitorial agents can make reputations for themselves without even realising it.

86.en: In theory, Inquisitors, with their limitless authority, can command armies and order planetary governors to do their bidding. In practice, plenty of planetary governors and military commanders might make things difficult if an Inquisitor makes unreasonable demands, especially if they work alone and might be considered a problem easily removed. Most Inquisitors would soon correct such attitudes, but none let such petty obstacles compromise a mission.

90.en: Imperial agents across the sector fear the Inquisition, but there are systems in the Macharian Sector where Imperial presence is minimal or completely absent. An Inquisitor might have to bring Imperial forces with them rather than rely on the compliance of the locals or simply work alone. While working alone presents challenges, it appeals to those Inquisitors who are reluctant to trust anyone during the ongoing shadow war. A solitary operation can also be an advantage for undercover work. @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.5jO3tXI5hSEBAC4s]{Infractionists} often actively resist Imperial rule and Imperial agents of all kinds, including Inquisitors. Inquisitorial agents might have to conceal their true identities and even stoop to making dangerous deals with criminals to gain information — especially those tracking aspects of the Silent Trade.

100.en: There are several wealthy, powerful, and well-travelled @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.h6Z6Ia2q5RkRUlDG]{Rogue Trader Dynasties} in the Macharian Sector. They travel across the sector and beyond Imperial space, especially from the borders of the Cytheris Subsector. Many captains claim noble lineage, and their ancient warrants grant them freedoms most citizens can only imagine. They are still obliged to bow to the authority of the Inquisition of course, but some might overlook this when encountering a single Inquisitorial agent, alone in the void. Far from civilisation, authority means little in the face of a gun.

110.en: Given the turbulent nature of the Macharian Sector, the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.cvpsLwcsXf4myIpK]{Adeptus Administratum} and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.6Yav4onpokz5e5jg]{Astra Militarum} work closely together. Inquisitorial authority is greater than either, but an Inquisitor might require the cooperation of both in their work. Between them, the Administratum are responsible for the smooth running of the sector. While the Administratum’s influence in the Macharian Sector is not as universal as it once was, the Astra Militarum’s power seems to have grown since the Noctis Aeterna, with its close ties to the @UUID[Compendium.impmal-starter-set.journals.JournalEntry.WE1MLa1KVRHMD8wJ.JournalEntryPage.P8rukYyQeyPJ1ubs]{Imperial Navy} and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.HURMpEU0Nnc93Ocv]{Adeptus Ministorum}. The Astra Militarum may be the most powerful organisation in this sector, and they are generally on good terms with the Inquisition. Inquisitors would do well to nurture contacts within this organisation. But some may believe that the Militarum has grown too influential here and would refuse to bow to Inquisitorial authority if there was a disagreement. However, this has not yet been a problem, as their goals typically align.

120.en: Inquisitors, especially of the Ordo Hereticus, work closely with the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.upGG1JZPDbC7dpJJ]{Adeptus Astra Telepathica} since both work to identify psykers and contain them. In the Macharian Sector, the work of the Adeptus Astra Telepathica has been made more difficult by problems with communications, transport routes, and the growing number of psykers. Inquisitors are actively trying to ease the growing burden on the Black Ships, and ties are particularly close between the Inquisition and Adeptus Astra Telepathica.

124.en: Inquisitors may well encounter the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.CBLdHnFWFqdhfRKx]{Sisters of Silence} in the Macharian Sector since their work on the Black Ships carries them all across the Imperium. Elite psyker hunters, their mission is to collect and transport unsanctioned psykers for the Astra Telepathica. This task often causes them to work alongside Inquisitorial agents of the Ordo Hereticus. They are useful allies, immune to psychic and daemonic power, as long as an Inquisitor's purpose remains aligned with theirs.

134.en: The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.9frbPZ9v3lFR9Kva]{Adeptus Mechanicus} is afforded greater freedom under the ancient Treaty of Mars than most factions within the Imperium are premitted. This has often been a point of contention between the Inquisition and the Cult Mechanicus, in the Macharian Sector as elsewhere. Several of the sector's forge worlds are under surveillance, and many Tech-Priests are aware of these intrusions, further souring relations.

144.en: The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.HURMpEU0Nnc93Ocv]{Adeptus Ministorum} is generally grateful for the work of the Inquisition since both organisations are united in their devotion to the God-Emperor above all else. The Ministorum is quite powerful in the Macharian Sector, at least among those worlds that the Astra Militarum has successfully repacified since the Noctis Aeterna. Nevertheless, some Inquisitors see the obsession with the Saint Solar Macharius as dangerous. On some worlds, the saint seems to receive more devotion than the God-Emperor. More than one member of the Adeptus Ministorum is currently under suspicion of encouraging such behaviour, and the local Adeptus Ministorum bristles at the implication that it requires such scrutiny.

152.en: Every sector, subsector, and world of the Imperium has its own set of laws, but the Lex Imperialis sits above these laws, consisting of the God-Emperor’s own word and must take precedence. It is a vast, complicated, and ever-growing collection of decrees and mandates, so numerous that most citizens of the Imperium could never hope to learn them all.

156.en: Theoretically, Inquisitors function above local laws, remaining bound only by the Lex Imperialis. However, by respecting local laws, Inquisitors are more likely to find planetary governors and local rulers more cooperative and avoid trouble with local enforcement. After all, most enforcers, such as the ubiquitous @UUID[Compendium.impmal-starter-set.actors.Actor.O49jTi2TzoFQH5GT]{Macharian Vigilites}, answer directly to their planetary governor. Adhering to the letter of the Lex also makes challenges from other Inquisitors less likely

160.en: It is the Inquisitor’s duty to enforce Imperial Law wherever they can. If a world resists the Imperium for no reason other than its leaders’ greed, then an Inquisitor is likely to inform the Arbites and leave them to their work. Sometimes, a world resists for more nefarious reasons: the workings of a daemonic cult, the foul promises of a Chaos God, or the influence of a powerful, unsanctioned psyker. In these cases, an Inquisitor’s presence and authority are necessary, drawing together the Imperium’s forces and applying their knowledge in combatting such a threat.

164.en: The enforcement of the Lex Imperialis is necessary for the continued existence of the Imperium through its bearing on the Imperial Tithe. Imperial worlds must all pay a tithe to the Emperor, whether in crops, troops, materiel, or captured psykers for the League of Black Ships. Obedience in this matter is non-negotiable, as from the perspective of the Inquisition, all should understand that the God-Emperor’s tithe benefits all. Yet, in the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96]{Macharian Sector}, there are still worlds that resist the Emperor’s rule and are lax with what they provide.

168.en: Given that the Imperium is stretched so far across the galaxy, it is easy for a planet’s indiscretions to be overlooked for a considerable time as long as they pay their tithe. Many worlds, particularly after a period of turbulence, might forget the Lex Imperialis’ importance. The arrival of Imperial agents, such as an Inquisitor, should be enough to remind them. In these cases, local governance may attempt to conceal evidence of their infringements, and it is up to the Inquisitor to determine whether these are petty crimes that can be ignored, dangerous violations that must be forcefully dealt with, or instead used as leverage to further their goals.

172.en: Most worlds are likely to deal with some element of criminality in their society. Some citizens live outside the law, using secrecy to avoid detection or bribes to avoid punishment. Others might even use knowledge of the Lex Imperialis to their advantage, especially if it can override local laws they might otherwise fall foul of. An Inquisitor who needs to circumvent the law may use similar tactics as necessary, especially if they are attempting to conceal their identity as an Inquisitor or those of their acolytes.

180.en: , it is up to the GM to decide how much of an obstacle local enforcers will be to the characters’ mission. On one world, a citizen’s activities might be severely limited by arbitrary local laws, while on another, chaotic lawlessness might make the characters' activities dangerous. Inquisitorial agents are likely to find their authority respected on some worlds, whereas on others, they would be wise to keep their associations to themselves. The prevalence of Imperial Law on all these worlds means that Chaos or xenos cults, unsanctioned psykers, and criminal enterprises are all likely to work in secret and outside of the law. However, there may be worlds where the local law enforcers, the government, or noble houses are corrupt, and the characters must actively break local laws to obey Imperial ones.

188.en: As they serve only the Emperor, answering to no other authority, Inquisitors must watch each other for signs of corruption. A traitorous Inquisitor is a hazardous thing, and it is the duty of all Inquisitors to police each other. Unfortunately, since Inquisitors vary so much in their philosophies and methods, what is considered heresy by one is considered necessary by another. After enemies of the Imperium, the greatest threat to an Inquisitor is another Inquisitor.

192.en: An Inquisitor who suspects another of corruption or treason may deal with the matter personally if they can. If they are not certain or not confident in their ability to capture or kill the Inquisitor in question, they may call upon other Inquisitors to form a Conclave and discuss the matter. Depending on the power and influence of the Inquisitors involved, this may be a small group whose existence will remain a secret or a grander assemblage, including Inquisitor Lords.

202.en: The Conclave investigates the suspect and then debates the best way to proceed. The Inquisitor may be called upon to defend themself personally or be kept unaware of the Conclave’s existence. There is no set procedure to follow since every case, and the threats involved, will differ. If in doubt, the Conclave often decides that in the best interests of the Imperium, the Inquisitor must be eliminated since a corrupt Inquisitor is an incredibly dangerous threat.

206.en: These wars must be fought in the shadows of the Imperium. The factions of the Adeptus Terra learning of an Inquisitor’s betrayals or shifts towards heresy undermines the limitless authority they need to protect the Imperium. An Inquisition that appears in any way divided is therefore ineffective. The same goes for the citizenry; though fear aids in asserting their authority, Inquisitors should never be seen as outright enemies of Lex-abiding people.
